cards.q: What is an electric field?
cards.a: A region in which a charged particle experiences a force.

cards.q: Define electric field strength at a point, and state its direction.
cards.a: The force per unit positive charge at that point: \(E = \frac{F}{Q}\). Its direction is the direction of the force on a positive charge. Unit: \(\text{N C}^{-1}\).

cards.q: State Coulomb's law.
cards.a: The force between two point charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: \(F = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Q_{1}Q_{2}}{r^{2}}\).
cards.why: Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

cards.q: Two point charges of \(2.0\ \mu\text{C}\) each are 0.30 m apart in air. Calculate the force between them. (\(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{C}^{-2}\))
cards.a: 0.40 N
cards.why: Forgetting to square the separation is the most common slip.

cards.q: When using Coulomb's law for a charged sphere in air, what two simplifications are made?
cards.a: The charge on the sphere is treated as if it were all at the centre, and air is treated as a vacuum.

cards.q: Calculate the ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force between two protons. (\(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\); \(m_{p} = 1.67 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}\); \(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\); \(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\), SI units)
cards.a: About \(1.2 \times 10^{36}\)
steps: Both forces vary as \(\frac{1}{r^{2}}\), so the separation cancels in the ratio.
cards.why: Gravity is negligible between subatomic particles.

cards.q: Write the equation for the electric field strength between two parallel plates.
cards.a: \(E = \frac{V}{d}\), where \(V\) is the potential difference between the plates and \(d\) their separation. Unit: \(\text{V m}^{-1}\).
cards.why: The field between the plates is uniform: the same everywhere.

cards.q: Derive \(E = \frac{V}{d}\) for a uniform field by considering the work done moving a charge \(Q\) between the plates.
cards.a: \(E = \frac{V}{d}\)
steps: Work done moving the charge across is force × distance: \(W = Fd\).
It is also charge × potential difference: \(W = QV\).

cards.q: A potential difference of 500 V is applied across parallel plates 0.020 m apart. Calculate the field strength between them.
cards.a: \(2.5 \times 10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}\)

cards.q: Calculate the force on an electron in a uniform field of strength \(2.5 \times 10^{4}\ \text{V m}^{-1}\). (\(e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}\))
cards.a: \(4.0 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{N}\)
cards.why: The force on an electron is opposite to the field direction, because its charge is negative.

cards.q: A charged particle enters a uniform electric field at right angles to the field. Describe its path, and explain why.
cards.a: A parabola. Its velocity along its original direction is constant, while it has a constant acceleration in the direction of the force, just like a projectile under gravity.

cards.q: Write the equation for the electric field strength at a distance \(r\) from a point charge \(Q\).
cards.a: \(E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Q}{r^{2}}\)

cards.q: Calculate the electric field strength 0.10 m from a point charge of 5.0 nC. (\(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{C}^{-2}\))
cards.a: \(4.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{N C}^{-1}\)

cards.q: Describe the electric field lines around an isolated positive point charge, and between two oppositely charged parallel plates.
cards.a: Point charge: radial, pointing away from the charge. Parallel plates: parallel and equally spaced, from the positive plate to the negative plate.
cards.why: Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive charge.

cards.q: Define electric potential at a point.
cards.a: The work done per unit positive charge in moving a small positive charge from infinity to that point. Unit: V (\(\text{J C}^{-1}\)).

cards.q: Write the equation for the electric potential at a distance \(r\) from a point charge \(Q\).
cards.a: \(V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}}\frac{Q}{r}\)
cards.why: The sign of the potential follows the sign of the charge: positive near a positive charge, negative near a negative one.

cards.q: Calculate the electric potential 0.10 m from a point charge of 5.0 nC. (\(\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_{0}} = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{C}^{-2}\))
cards.a: 450 V

cards.q: How much work is done moving a charge \(Q\) through a potential difference \(\Delta V\)?
cards.a: \(\Delta W = Q\Delta V\)
cards.why: No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential, where \(\Delta V = 0\).

cards.q: How is electric field strength related to the way potential changes with distance?
cards.a: Field strength is the potential gradient: \(E = \frac{\Delta V}{\Delta r}\) in magnitude, and the field points in the direction in which the potential falls.
cards.why: Where equipotentials are close together, the field is strong.

cards.q: What does the area under a graph of electric field strength \(E\) against distance \(r\) represent?
cards.a: The potential difference between the two distances.

cards.q: Define capacitance, and state its unit.
cards.a: The charge stored per unit potential difference: \(C = \frac{Q}{V}\). Unit: the farad, F.

cards.q: A \(470\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor is charged to 12 V. Calculate the charge stored.
cards.a: \(5.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{C}\)

cards.q: Write the equation for the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor, and say what each symbol means.
cards.a: \(C = \frac{A\varepsilon_{0}\varepsilon_{r}}{d}\): \(A\) the area of overlap of the plates, \(d\) their separation, \(\varepsilon_{0}\) the permittivity of free space, \(\varepsilon_{r}\) the relative permittivity of the material between them.

cards.q: Two plates of area \(0.020\ \text{m}^{2}\) are 1.0 mm apart in air. Calculate the capacitance. (\(\varepsilon_{0} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F m}^{-1}\); take \(\varepsilon_{r} = 1\))
cards.a: \(1.8 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{F}\)

cards.q: What is the relative permittivity (dielectric constant) of a material?
cards.a: The factor by which the capacitance increases when the material completely fills the space between the plates, compared with a vacuum.

cards.q: Explain how a dielectric made of polar molecules increases the capacitance of a capacitor.
cards.a: Its molecules line up and set up a field that opposes the field between the plates.
marks: The polar molecules rotate in the electric field so that they line up with it.
Their charges produce an electric field in the opposite direction to the field between the plates.
This reduces the overall field, and so the potential difference, for the same charge on the plates.
\(C = \frac{Q}{V}\): a smaller potential difference for the same charge means a larger capacitance.

cards.q: Write three equivalent expressions for the energy stored by a capacitor.
Use the graph of potential difference against charge for a capacitor to show that the energy stored is \(\frac{1}{2}QV\).
steps: \(V = \frac{Q}{C}\), so the graph of \(V\) against \(Q\) is a straight line through the origin.
The work done adding a small charge \(\Delta Q\) at potential difference \(V\) is \(V\Delta Q\): a thin strip of area under the graph.
The total work done is the whole area under the graph: a triangle.
cards.why: The half is there because the potential difference rises from zero as the capacitor charges.

cards.q: Calculate the energy stored by a \(470\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor charged to 12 V.
cards.a: 0.034 J

cards.q: What is the time constant of a resistor–capacitor circuit?
cards.a: \(RC\): the time taken for the charge (or the potential difference, or the current) of a discharging capacitor to fall to \(\frac{1}{e}\), about 37%, of its initial value.

cards.q: A \(470\ \mu\text{F}\) capacitor discharges through a \(10\ \text{k}\Omega\) resistor. Calculate the time constant.
cards.a: 4.7 s

cards.q: Write the equation for the charge on a capacitor discharging through a resistor. Which other quantities follow the same equation?
cards.a: \(Q = Q_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\). The potential difference and the current decay in the same way: \(V = V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\) and \(I = I_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\).

cards.q: A capacitor charged to 12 V discharges through a resistor. The time constant is 4.7 s. Calculate the potential difference across it after 10 s.
cards.a: 1.4 V

cards.q: A capacitor discharges with a time constant of 2.0 s. Calculate the time taken for its charge to fall to half its initial value.
cards.a: 1.4 s
cards.why: 0.69 is \(\ln 2\): setting \(Q = \frac{1}{2}Q_{0}\) in the discharge equation gives \(t = RC\ln 2\).

cards.q: Write the equation for the charge on a capacitor as it charges through a resistor.
cards.a: \(Q = Q_{0}\left(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\right)\), where \(Q_{0}\) is the final charge.
cards.why: The potential difference across the capacitor rises in the same way. The current does not: it decays exponentially.

cards.q: A capacitor is charging through a resistor. A student writes the current as \(I = I_{0}\left(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\right)\). What is wrong?
cards.a: While charging, the current decays from its initial value: \(I = I_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\). Only the charge and the potential difference across the capacitor follow the rising \(1 - e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\) form.

cards.q: Explain why the current falls as a capacitor charges through a resistor from a fixed supply.
cards.a: The growing potential difference across the capacitor leaves less across the resistor.
marks: As charge builds up on the plates, the potential difference across the capacitor rises.
The supply potential difference is shared between the capacitor and the resistor.
So the potential difference across the resistor falls.
\(I = \frac{V}{R}\), so the current falls, reaching zero when the capacitor is fully charged.

cards.q: For a capacitor circuit, what does the gradient of a charge–time graph represent, and the area under a current–time graph?
cards.a: Gradient of charge–time: the current. Area under current–time: the charge that has flowed.

cards.q: For a discharging capacitor, what graph gives a straight line, and how is the time constant found from it?
cards.a: \(\ln V\) against \(t\). Its gradient is \(-\frac{1}{RC}\), so \(RC = -\frac{1}{\text{gradient}}\).
cards.why: Taking logs of \(V = V_{0}e^{-\frac{t}{RC}}\) gives \(\ln V = \ln V_{0} - \frac{t}{RC}\).

answerFigure.alt: The natural logarithm of potential difference against time for a discharging capacitor: a straight line sloping downwards.

cards.q: Outline how to determine the time constant of a capacitor discharging through a resistor.
cards.a: Record the potential difference as the capacitor discharges and plot a log graph.
marks: Charge the capacitor from a supply, then switch it to discharge through a resistor.
Record the potential difference across the capacitor at regular times, with a data logger, an oscilloscope, or a voltmeter and stopwatch.
Plot \(\ln V\) against \(t\): a straight line.
The gradient is \(-\frac{1}{RC}\), so the time constant is \(-\frac{1}{\text{gradient}}\).

cards.q: After how many time constants is a discharging capacitor usually treated as fully discharged?
cards.a: About five: by then less than 1% of the initial charge remains.
